source_text: Constat autem non esse apostolicorum verborum eum ordinem, quem inimicus noster putavit. Argumentatur quippe hoc modo: Si Apostolus imitationem, inquit, voluisset intellegi, non " per unum hominem " [n89] , sed per diabolum peccatum intrasse, et per omnes homines pertransisse dixisset. De diabolo quippe scriptum est: " Imitantur eum, qui sunt ex parte eius " [n90] . Sed ideo " per unum hominem " dixit, a quo generatio utique hominum coepit ut per generationem doceret isse per omnes originale peccatum [n91] . In hoc ergo mentitur, quod affirmat beatum Paulum pronuntiasse, quia per unum hominem peccatum intraverit in mundum, atque ita in omnes homines pertransierit; hoc, inquam, in Magistri Gentium sermonibus non tenetur; ille quippe non dixit peccatum transisse, sed mortem. Est ergo ordo verborum: Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum intravit, et per peccatum mors; et ita in omnes homines pertransiit, in quo omnes peccaverunt [n92] . Sublimis informator Ecclesiae, quid sibi dicendum esset expendit: Per unum, inquit, hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors; et ita in omnes homines pertransiit. Iam nominaverat mortem, atque peccatum; quid fuit necesse ut in eo quod pertransisse dicebat, mortem a peccati communione separaret, ut signanter ostenderet, in hunc quidem mundum per unum hominem intrasse peccatum, et per peccatum mortem; in omnes vero homines non peccatum transisse, sed mortem, utique iudicii illatam severitate, praevaricationis ultricem, non corporum semina, sed morum vitia persequentem; nisi quia commendare et praemunire curavit, ne vestro dogmati opitulatus aliquid putaretur?
pass_a_gloss: But it stands that that order of apostolic words is not which our enemy thought. For he argues in this way: If the Apostle, he says, had wanted imitation to be understood, he would have said that sin entered not 'through one human being' but through the devil, and passed through all human beings. For of the devil it is written: 'They imitate him, who are from his party.' But for this reason he said 'through one human being,' from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, that he might teach that original sin went through all by generation. In this therefore he lies, that he affirms that blessed Paul pronounced that through one human being sin entered into the world, and so passed through into all human beings; this, I say, is not held in the speeches of the Teacher of the Gentiles; for he did not say that sin passed, but death. The order of words is therefore: Just as through one human being sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed through into all human beings, in whom all sinned. The sublime informer of the Church weighed what ought to be said by him: Through one, he says, human being sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed through into all human beings. He had already named death, and sin; what was necessary that in that which he was saying had passed through he should separate death from communion with sin, so that he might signally show that into this world indeed through one human being sin entered, and through sin death; but into all human beings not sin passed, but death, brought on at any rate by the severity of judgment, avenger of transgression, pursuing not the seeds of bodies but the vices of manners; except because he took care to commend and to fortify in advance, lest he be thought to have helped your dogma in anything?

pass_b_english: But the apostle’s words plainly do not have the sequence our enemy imagined. His argument runs like this: ‘If the apostle had meant imitation,’ he says, ‘he would have said that sin entered through the devil and passed through all human beings, rather than “through one man” (Romans 5:12). For Scripture says of the devil: “Those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24; Latin numbering 2:25). But he said “through one man,” from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, precisely to teach that original sin passed through all people by generation’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). His falsehood, then, lies in affirming that blessed Paul declared that sin entered the world through one man and so passed into all human beings. This, I repeat, is not found in the Teacher of the Gentiles’ words. Paul did not say sin passed on, but death. The sequence is: ‘Just as through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). The church’s exalted teacher weighed what he should say: ‘Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so it passed into all human beings.’ He had already named both death and sin. Why, in speaking of what passed on, did he need to separate death from association with sin? Why expressly show that sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin, but that what passed into all human beings was not sin but death—death imposed by the severity of judgment, avenging transgression, pursuing not bodily seed but moral faults? Surely because he took care to commend and safeguard his meaning, so that no one would suppose he had given any support to your doctrine.
